To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
male gender, BMI, blood triglycerides and blood viscosity are associated with relative hypertension, but not with the occurrence of acute complications, in adults with sickle cell anaemia.
male gender, elevated triglycerides, body mass index, and blood viscosity are independently associated with relative hypertension.
the following factors increase the risk for hypertension in sickle cell anema: male gender, increased body mass index, increased triglyceride levels and increased blood viscosity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the identification of biological markers of relative hypertension in Sickle Cell Disease, which may help to better understand the mechanisms underlying this complication.
the identification of biological factors associated with the occurrence of relative hypertension in Sickle Cell Disease.
the identification of biological factors associated with the occurrence of hypertension in SCA, which is a major risk factor for chronic and acute complications in this population.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
male gender, BMI, triglyceride level and blood viscosity could be considered as risk factors for relative hypertension and that triglyceride levels may also be a risk factor for vaso-occlusion.
the presence of hypertension is a marker of the severity of the sickle cell disease and not the cause.
the relative hypertension in Sickle cell anemia is a consequence of the interaction between the genetic background, the hematological and lipid profile and the hemodynamic factors.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the risk factors for relative hypertension and for acute complications in sickle cell disease are not the same.
relative hypertension and vaso-occlusion are associated with a similar set of risk factors in SCA.
relative hypertension in SCD is associated with a male gender, increased BMI, triglyceride levels and blood viscosity.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the risk for developing hypertension in sickle cell anemias should be considered as a risk factor for developing complications in sickle cell patients.
the risk for hypertension is increased in men, in overweight individuals and in individuals with high triglyceride levels.
patients with SCA should be screened for relative hypertension and that the management of relative hypertension should be a part of their care.
